children: Brazil's presidential election result is poised to hammer financial markets, with currency futures and exchange-traded funds tracking local stocks both tumbling in Asia trading.

Leftist candidate President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva managed to clinch an upset victory over right-wing contender Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday with over 99% of votes counted, according to local authorities.

The front-Month Brazilian real futures contract weakened nearly 10% against the dollar in early Asian trade Monday, according to CME data. Exchange-traded funds tracking Brazilian stocks trading in Japan and China were down between 10% and 14%.

A Bolsonaro win had been viewed as the more market-friendly outcome due to promises of fiscal consolidation, privatization, pro-business reforms, and expectations of closer alignment with the U.S., according to a report by Janus Henderson Investors earlier this month.

Brazilian equities had rallied sharply after the first electoral round gave a clear lead to Bolsonaro, before giving back modest gains as polls tightened during the runoff campaign, Goldman Sachs analysts said in note Friday.
Prediction markets had continued to favor Bolsonaro heading into the final vote.
In the wake of the upset, the U.S. dollar might post a 5% gap higher against the real, similar to the 5% gap lower observed after the first round, said Sean Callow, senior FX analyst at ITC.
After the expected jolt to asset prices on Monday, where they head after will likely depend on policy statements, GS economists said in the wake of the poll results.
A key point to watch will be cabinet posts: "For investors, first and foremost would be who would lead the Ministry of Finance," GS's Alberto Ramos and Panteleymon Semka said.
Eyes will also be on fiscal consolidation strategies.

Neither political camp gave very detailed proposals on that front, and the market will ultimately require policy execution rather than electoral signalling, said Thomas Haugaard, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors.

"A thorough, transparent accounting of the fiscal cost of campaign measures/promises--and of the revisions and adjustments required for the 2027 budget--is also essential," GS said. "Fiscal sustainability remains the primary pricing anchor for Brazilian sovereign risk."
In Goldman's view, major structural reforms seem unlikely under a fourth Lula term. GS anticipates modest measures to contain primary spending growth, and increases in an already high tax burden.
"The administration would likely retain its strong belief that the public sector and state-owned enterprises should remain central engines of growth and investment," GS said.
James Glynn contributed to this report
